topic: hand-painting a shop sign and gilding its letters with gold leaf

provenance.author: glowny-en-d
provenance.notes: 10 turns, user first; variant a is sign arithmetic (letters, leaves, books, coats, timings) with closed task questions, base is a dialogue about painting and gilding a bookshop sign. Grounded external referent: the drying rack by the window, introduced in turn 0 (the board rests on it between every stage) and mentioned in the sentence directly before every insertion.

a: Here is the work sheet for one shop sign, and its figures need going through in order.
The board measures thirty-six inches across by eighteen inches down on the face.
Line one carries twelve letters and line two carries eight, with an ornament between the lines.
Every letter takes two leaves of gold, and leaves come in books of twenty-five.
How many leaves of gold does the lettering call for across both lines together?
base: I am painting a hanging sign for my sister's bookshop, with gilded letters on a dark green field.
The board is primed, and the lettering is drawn out full size on paper.
Between coats the board lies on a slatted rack by the window, where the light is even.
I have never handled gold leaf before, though my brushwork on flat colour is steady.
What order should the remaining work follow so the gold goes on last and safest?

a: Twelve letters and eight letters make twenty letters across the two lines of the sign.
At two leaves for every letter the job calls for forty leaves of gold.
Forty leaves come out of two books of twenty-five, with ten leaves left over.
The board face is six hundred forty-eight square inches at the stated measurements.
Does the forty leaf figure match the total pencilled on the work sheet?
base: Finish every coat of the field colour first, because leaf sticks to any tacky paint it touches.
Rub down between coats lightly, and let each one harden well before the next.
Transfer the drawn letters only when the final field coat has cured hard.
Keep the board flat on the rack while paint dries, since runs ruin crisp edges.
Is the sign to hang outdoors in the weather, or inside the shop window?

a: Now work out the paint coats, because the field takes three coats of green.
Each coat needs twelve hours of drying before the next one can go on.
The two undercoats before the green each need the same twelve hours as well.
Painting a coat takes forty minutes of brush time on a board this size.
How many hours of drying do the five coats need from first to last?
base: The sign hangs outdoors on an iron bracket above the door, facing the street.
The rack by the window keeps each coat dust-free while it dries overnight.
I have three coats of green on now, and the surface feels glassy under my palm.
The paper pattern is pricked along every letter, ready for the pounce bag.
Which gold should an outdoor sign carry, transfer leaf or the loose kind?

a: Five coats at twelve hours each come to sixty hours of drying across the job.
The brush time adds two hundred minutes, which is three hours and twenty minutes.
Together the coats claim sixty-three hours and twenty minutes before any gilding starts.
Spread over days, that is a coat each morning and evening for two and a half days.
Is the sixty hour drying figure the one that goes into the calendar?
base: Outdoors, use transfer leaf in double thickness, because wind makes loose leaf a misery on a doorstep.
Twenty-three carat and above weathers well without any varnish over the gold.
Pounce the pattern, then paint the letters in the size with a steady writer's brush.
Set the board back on the rack while the size comes up to tack.
Have you got a soft gilder's mop for pressing the leaf down into the strokes?

a: One correction before the books are ordered, because the wording changed this morning.
Line one now carries ten letters instead of twelve, and line two stays at eight.
Recalculate the letter total, the leaves needed and the leaves left over from full books.
Keep the rule at two leaves for every letter as it stands on the sheet.
What does the leaf count become with ten letters on the first line?
base: I have ordered the double thickness transfer leaf and a mop from the supplier in town.
A correction to the layout I described, because the wording changed at my sister's request.
The sign now reads two lines rather than three, with a small ornament between them.
The rack will hold the board level tonight while the last green coat cures.
Does the shorter wording change how long the size should sit before the gold goes on?

a: Ten and eight make eighteen letters, so the lettering now calls for thirty-six leaves.
Thirty-six leaves still need two books of twenty-five, with fourteen leaves left over.
The spare margin grows by four leaves compared with the earlier count of forty.
Nothing else on the sheet moves, because the coats and the board are unchanged.
Should the fourteen spare leaves be kept against mends, or returned with the order?
base: The wording does not change the waiting, since tack depends on the size and the weather.
Test the tack with a knuckle: it should click softly without leaving any print.
Gild the top line first, working down so fallen skewings never land on wet size.
Overlap each leaf slightly, and press it home with the mop in small circles.
Can you keep the room still while you gild, with windows shut and no draughts?

a: Keep the spares against mends and move on to the gilding time next.
Gilding runs at six letters an hour once the size has come to tack.
The size itself needs ninety minutes from brushing on to being ready for gold.
The shadow lines afterwards run at ten letters an hour with the fine brush.
How long does gilding eighteen letters take at six letters an hour?
base: The room can be shut up tight, and I will gild early before the street wakes.
My first test letter on a scrap board came out bright with only two small breaks.
The breaks sit where my size went thin at the tail of the stroke.
Mending them with little patches of leaf worked, though the mend shows at an angle.
Will those faults disappear once the sign hangs high above the door?

a: Eighteen letters at six letters an hour take three hours of gilding time.
The ninety minutes of size tack brings the gilding stage to four and a half hours.
The shadow lines on eighteen letters take one hour and forty-eight minutes at ten an hour.
Rounded up, the shadow session goes on the sheet as two hours of brush time.
Is four and a half hours the figure entered for the gilding day?
base: Faults that show on the bench vanish at height, because nobody views a sign from a handspan away.
Even trade work carries small mends, and weather softens the gold's shine within a season.
Burnish nothing on an outdoor sign, since the matt surface reads better against dark paint.
Dust the finished letters with a soft cloth once everything has hardened for a week.
Do you plan an outline or shadow line to lift the letters off the green?

a: Now close the sheet with the full timeline from first undercoat to hanging day.
Stage one is the five coats, stage two the gilding, and stage three the shadows.
A week of hardening sits between the gilding and the shadow session on the plan.
Sealing the back and fitting the rings take one final morning at the end.
The order runs coats, gilding, hardening week, shadows and then the final morning.
base: A fine cream shadow line on the lower right of every letter is the plan.
I will paint the shadows a week after the gold, when the leaf has settled.
The ornament between the lines stays plain green and cream, without any gold at all.
My sister wants the sign up before the shop's tenth birthday at the end of the month.
For the first time I believe the board on that rack will be ready in time.

a: The five coats span two and a half days at the twelve hour spacing.
The gilding day adds four and a half hours, and the hardening adds seven days.
The shadow session adds two hours, and the final morning adds about three more.
End to end the sheet spans roughly eleven days from first coat to hanging.
The sign is ready inside the month with days to spare on the calendar.
base: Leave the shadow paint thin, because a heavy shadow line overpowers gold at street height.
Seal the back and edges of the board against rain before the bracket goes up.
Check the fixing rings and the bracket bolts once a year when the ladder is out.
Gold laid on sound size and left alone will outlast every painted part of that sign.
The tenth birthday deadline is comfortable if the coats keep drying at their present pace.
